visible.presentation_text:
Consult request from the member of the public who brought the animal to the facility.

Big brown bat, adult, admitted after a cat encounter. Wounds to the wing membrane and body wall have developed necrotizing infection consistent with *Pasteurella*; despite antibiotic therapy the infection has extended into the thoracic wall.

Bat has lost 34% of admission weight over nine days, is not self-feeding, tolerates assist-feeding poorly, and vocalizes continuously on handling. Wing membrane is necrotic across the majority of the right side and the process is advancing. Attending veterinarian reports the infection is not responding, the tissue loss is not survivable, and distress is not controlled.

Bat is non-releasable. Bats are a rabies vector species in Massachusetts. Live RVS animals are not authorized for educational programming, and transfer options are correspondingly narrow. No breeding or research use is available to this facility.

Permanent captivity requires a small enclosure with roosting structure, daily hand-feeding of mealworms, and hibernation management. Housing and feeding costs are minimal; the enclosure occupies little space. Big brown bats can live 15 years or more in captivity, and this individual would be maintained with the facility's two other permanent bats.
menu_options: Continue permanent care at the facility
Transfer the animal to a permitted bat facility
